text: What does sound need to propagate, unlike light and X-rays?
options: A material medium, such as water or soft tissue

text: What type of waves does sound consist of?

options: Perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation
Parallel to the direction of wave propagation
In a circular motion around their equilibrium position

text: What are the regions where particles of the medium come closer together during the passage of a longitudinal sound wave?
How is sound defined physically according to the properties of ultrasound?
options: A flow of electrons through an electrical conductor
A pressure disturbance (vibration) that propagates through matter

text: Through which of the following states of matter can sound waves travel?
options: All states of matter (gases, liquids, solids, and plasma)

text: What type of energy do the mechanical pressure waves of sound carry as they propagate?
Why can sound not travel through a vacuum?
options: Because a vacuum reflects all sound waves
Because sound requires a material medium to propagate as a mechanical pressure wave
Because a vacuum immediately absorbs the kinetic energy of the wave
Because sound travels at the speed of light in a vacuum

text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the nature of sound wave propagation?
options: They propagate as electromagnetic waves that do not require a medium
They propagate as mechanical pressure waves
They propagate only through crystalline solids
They propagate by transferring matter itself from one place to another

text: According to the physical definition, what is the minimum frequency at which sound is classified as ultrasound?
What does the term "Ultrasounds" refer to when applied to sound?
options: Sounds that travel faster than the speed of sound in air
Any frequencies above the range of human hearing (audible sound)
Very loud sounds that damage the human ear

text: What is the frequency range actually used in medical ultrasound imaging devices?
What is the primary purpose of using diagnostic medical ultrasound?
options: To help diagnose and treat patients using high-frequency sound
To heat deep tissues in the body using ionizing radiation
To measure the electrical activity of the heart and brain
To sterilize internal tissues from bacteria and viruses

text: What does "SONAR" stand for?
Which of the following materials is mentioned as an example of natural crystals with piezoelectric properties?
What is the commonly used synthetic material with piezoelectric properties, known by the abbreviation PZT (Ceramic)?
What atomic structural feature gives piezoelectric crystals their unique electrical properties?
options: The presence of free electrons that move completely freely
The absence of any electrical charges within atoms

text: In describing piezoelectric crystals, what does the phrase "two reciprocal abilities" referring to the abilities of these crystals mean?
options: Converting sound energy into thermal energy only
Reversible conversion between electrical signals and mechanical (sound) waves
Storing electrical charges for long periods without loss

text: What are the input and output of piezoelectric crystals, and what is the input in the "Direct Effect"?
options: Input: Electrical charge → Output: Mechanical strain
Input: Mechanical strain (compression or tension) → Output: Electrical charge (voltage)

text: Which of the following functions in an ultrasound device primarily depends on the "Direct Effect"?
options: Transmitting sound pulses into the body
Receiving echoes and converting them into electrical signals
Magnifying the image on the screen

text: When mechanical strain is applied to a piezoelectric crystal, how is electrical charge generated?
options: By heating the crystal until electrons are emitted from it
By the separation of positive and negative charges within the material as a result of compression or tension
By connecting the crystal to a powerful external energy source
By a chemical reaction occurring on the surface of the crystal

text: In addition to crystals and ceramics, which of the following biological materials were mentioned in the text as showing an electrical charge response when subjected to mechanical strain?
What is another name for "Process II" mentioned in the title (Electrical Charge ⇒ Mechanical Strain)?
When does the "Inverse Effect" occur in the context of an ultrasound device?
options: When the crystal receives the echo returning from the tissues
When an electrical charge is applied to the crystal, causing it to vibrate and produce sound waves
When the crystal is exposed to high temperatures
When the crystal breaks due to severe pressure

text: As stated in the text, what is the basic structure of an ultrasound transducer?
options: A single piezoelectric crystal surrounded only by a layer of plastic
A piezoelectric crystal or elements sandwiched between two metal plates
An electrical coil placed inside an evacuated glass tube
A permanent magnet surrounded by a copper coil

text: On which physical property does the transducer primarily depend for its function?
What happens when a sound wave strikes the metal plates of the transducer during the "Reception" or "Listening" stage?
options: The metal plates melt and turn into liquid
The plates vibrate, and the crystal picks up this mechanical vibration and converts it into a weak alternating electrical voltage (weak AC voltage)
The vibrations stop completely and the crystal absorbs the energy without moving
The sound energy is converted directly into visible light

text: What does the piezoelectric crystal produce when it picks up the mechanical vibration caused by a sound wave striking it?
options: A strong direct current (strong DC current)
A weak alternating electrical voltage (weak AC voltage)

text: Why are the plates fixed in the transducer structure used, according to the simplified description in the text?
options: Because they act as a permanent electrical insulator
Because they vibrate when struck by sound waves and transmit the vibration to the crystal
Because they always supply electricity from outside the crystal
Because they prevent sound waves from leaving the device

text: What does the basic structure of an ultrasound transducer consist of?
options: A copper coil and a permanent magnet
Piezoelectric crystals sandwiched between two metal plates
A glass lens and a laser light source
A discharge tube and a phosphor screen

text: When a sound wave strikes the two metal plates of a transducer, what happens to the piezoelectric crystal located between them?
options: The crystal melts and turns into liquid
The crystal picks up the mechanical vibration and converts it into a weak alternating electrical voltage (weak AC voltage)
The crystal reflects the sound without any change in its energy
The crystal generates high heat that breaks the two metal plates

text: Into what type of energy is mechanical (sound) energy converted during the "Reception" or "Listening" process inside the transducer?
What is the essential and fundamental component of every ultrasound transducer?
How many main functions does the piezoelectric crystal perform inside the transducer?
options: Two main functions (producing pulses and receiving echoes)
Three functions (transmission, reception, and image processing)
Four functions (transmission, reception, storage, and printing)

text: What is the first function mentioned for the piezoelectric crystal in the transducer?
options: Displaying the final image on the screen

text: What is the second function of the piezoelectric crystal after transmitting pulses?
options: Amplifying electrical signals from the main source
Receiving or detecting the returning echoes
Generating a magnetic field to image tissues

text: Why is the piezoelectric crystal considered a vital component in ultrasound imaging?
options: Because it performs a dual function, acting as both a transmitter and a receiver of sound waves
Because it prevents sound from leaving the patient’s body
Because it converts electricity into light only
Because it electronically controls the storage of patient data

options: Because they operate at very high frequencies exceeding 15 MHz
Because they fit the narrow spaces between the ribs due to their small footprint
Because they produce only static images and are unsuitable for motion
Because they are large and cover a wide area of the body at once

text: Which of the following medical applications is mentioned as a major use of sector transducers because of the small "acoustic windows"?
options: Imaging superficial blood vessels in the arm

text: According to the text, why are convex or curved transducers usually used for abdominal viewing?
options: Because they provide better resolution and penetration benefits
Because they are the least expensive among all transducers
